stem: What are the correct VHF Channels and Frequencies for Calling/Distress, DSC and bridge-to-bridge operations?
explanation: Channel 16 (156.800 MHz) is the international voice distress, safety and calling channel, Channel 70 (156.525 MHz) is reserved exclusively for digital selective calling, and Channel 13 (156.650 MHz) is the bridge-to-bridge navigation safety channel used between vessels.

stem: What is the frequency separation between Transmit and Receive frequencies on a duplex channel?
choices: 2.8 MHz
4.6 MHz
6.4 MHz
10.7 MHz
explanation: Marine VHF duplex channels pair a ship transmit frequency with a coast station transmit frequency 4.6 MHz higher. On Channel 26, for example, ships transmit on 157.300 MHz and the coast station on 161.900 MHz: 161.900 − 157.300 = 4.6 MHz.

stem: What is the assigned channel spacing for VHF channels?
choices: 10 kHz
15 kHz
25 kHz
50 kHz
explanation: Marine VHF channels sit on a 25 kHz raster. Consecutively numbered channels are 50 kHz apart and the 60-series channels fall halfway between them; Channel 70 at 156.525 MHz, for example, sits between Channel 10 (156.500 MHz) and Channel 11 (156.550 MHz).

stem: What is the allowed frequency tolerance for the DSC carrier frequencies?
choices: 10 Hz
20 Hz
5 ppm
10 ppm
explanation: VHF ship transmitters, including DSC on Channel 70, must hold their carrier within 10 parts per million. At 156.525 MHz that allows 156.525 MHz × 10×10⁻⁶ ≈ 1565 Hz of error either way.

stem: Using a frequency counter with an accuracy of 2 ppm — which of the following are within legal tolerance for the frequencies of 156.800 MHz and 156.525 MHz?
explanation: The counter itself may be off by 2 ppm, so a reading is only certainly legal if it lies within 10 − 2 = 8 ppm: 156.800 MHz × 8×10⁻⁶ ≈ 1254 Hz and 156.525 MHz × 8×10⁻⁶ ≈ 1252 Hz. Readings 1242 Hz low and 1243 Hz high both pass.

stem: Using a frequency counter with an accuracy of 5 ppm — which of the following are within legal tolerance for the frequencies of 156.875 MHz and 157.200?
explanation: Subtract the counter's 5 ppm uncertainty from the 10 ppm limit, leaving 5 ppm: 156.875 MHz × 5×10⁻⁶ ≈ 784 Hz and 157.200 MHz × 5×10⁻⁶ = 786 Hz. Readings 774 Hz high and 679 Hz low are the only pair inside both limits.

stem: What is the purpose of the USA-INT switch?
choices: To provide for simplex operations with European Public Correspondence stations.
To provide for duplex operations with U.S. Public Correspondence stations.
To change from duplex to simplex operation on designated channels in European waters.
To change from duplex to simplex operation on designated channels in U.S. waters.
explanation: Some channels that are duplex under the international plan are used simplex in U.S. waters, with ships and coast stations both on the ship transmit frequency (Channel 22A for Coast Guard liaison is the best-known). The USA setting switches those channels to simplex so the radio matches U.S. assignments.

stem: What may happen if the USA-INT control is left on INT when in U.S. waters?
choices: Your signals will be heard but other station replies will not be heard on certain channels.
You will be able to communicate with public correspondence stations on Channel 5.
Other stations will not be able to hear your transmissions and you will not hear any signals.
You will not be able to operate on channel 13.
explanation: In INT mode, certain channels that are simplex in the U.S. operate duplex: the radio transmits on the ship frequency but listens 4.6 MHz higher. Other stations hear your call, but their replies on the simplex frequency never reach your receiver.

stem: What is the purpose of the Dual Watch function?
choices: Allows simultaneous reception on two different channels.
To rapidly switch the radio’s receiver between two channels.
Allows reception and transmission at the same time.
It allows you to monitor both sides of a public correspondence station’s communication.
explanation: Dual watch lets a single receiver cover Channel 16 plus one other channel by switching back and forth rapidly, sampling each in turn. It doesn't receive both at once, which would take two receivers, and it has nothing to do with transmitting.

stem: What is the proper adjustment of the squelch control for maximum sensitivity?
choices: Maximum clockwise rotation.
Maximum counterclockwise rotation.
Just below the point where the noise breaks through.
The squelch has no effect on the sensitivity.
explanation: Squelch sets the signal level needed to open the audio. Advancing it only to the threshold where background noise is just silenced keeps the receiver quiet while still letting the weakest signals through; turning it further raises the threshold and blocks weak stations.

stem: Which of the following transmitter power levels are permitted by FCC rules?
choices: Low Power: 0.1 W, High Power: 5 W
Low Power: 0.5 W, High Power: 25 W
Low Power: 1 W, High Power: 25 W
Low Power: 5 W, High Power: 50 W
explanation: FCC rules limit VHF marine ship transmitters to 25 W and require that power can be reduced to 1 W or less. The low setting is used for short-range calls such as harbor and bridge-to-bridge communications, keeping interference to a minimum.

stem: Which of the following controls is not found on a VHF-DSC transceiver?
choices: “Distress”
“Cancel”
“Squelch”
explanation: R.I.T. (receiver incremental tuning) fine-tunes the receive frequency on MF/HF single-sideband sets. Channelized VHF FM radios have no need for it, while distress, cancel and squelch controls are standard on a VHF-DSC transceiver.

stem: Which of the following best describes the “Capture effect?”
choices: The receiver will accept all signals near the operating frequency.
The receiver will reject all but the weakest signal.
The receiver will reject all but the strongest signal.
The receiver will modulate an adjacent transmitter.
explanation: When two FM signals share a channel, the limiter and detector lock onto the stronger one and suppress the weaker, often completely if one is just a few dB stronger. This capture effect is why an FM receiver delivers only the strongest signal.

stem: Which of the following may be adjusted in a FM ratio detector for improved signal-to-noise?
choices: The diode detector
Input signal to the two diodes
Input voltage to the transistor
Ratio Arm balance control bridge
explanation: A ratio detector's output depends on the ratio of the voltages developed in its two diode arms, so amplitude variations tend to cancel. Adjusting the balance of those ratio arms equalizes the two halves, maximizing AM noise rejection and improving signal-to-noise.

stem: What is the function of a properly adjusted limiter circuit?
choices: Maintains a constant output amplitude with a varying input amplitude.
Limits the level of RF output power in the final amplifier stage.
Limits the modulation input amplitude while amplifying the modulation output.
Controls the DC input voltage excursions of the final amplifier stage.
explanation: A limiter is driven into saturation, so its output stays at a constant amplitude however much the input varies. That strips amplitude noise and fading from the FM signal before the detector, which only needs the frequency variations.

stem: Which of the following are true about SINAD measurements?
choices: SINAD is the product of the signal and noise divided by the sum of the noise and distortion.
SINAD is the sum of the signal, noise and distortion divided by the sum of the noise and distortion.
SINAD is the sum of the noise and distortion divided by the sum of the signal, noise and distortion.
SINAD is the product of the noise and distortion divided by the sum of the signal and noise.
explanation: SINAD compares everything at the receiver's audio output with the unwanted part: SINAD = (signal + noise + distortion) ÷ (noise + distortion), usually expressed in dB. A 12 dB SINAD reading is the common reference point for FM receiver sensitivity.

stem: What would be considered a normal sensitivity for 10 db of quieting in a VHF marine receiver?
choices: 0.1 microvolt
1 microvolt
5 microvolts
10 microvolts
explanation: A healthy marine VHF receiver should reach 10 dB of quieting with roughly 1 µV of signal at its antenna input. If it takes 5 or 10 µV to quiet the receiver that much, its sensitivity is poor and the front end should be checked.

stem: What is meant by “full quieting” in a FM VHF receiver?
choices: Adjusting the squelch control to eliminate background noise.
The rapid decrease in SINAD and noise with increasing signal level.
The received signal is strong enough to completely quiet the receiver background noise.
The rapid improvement in SINAD and decrease in noise with decreasing signal level.
explanation: Full quieting means the incoming signal is strong enough to drive the limiters fully into saturation, so the receiver's background hiss disappears completely and only clean audio remains. It describes signal strength, not a squelch setting.

stem: What condition may prevent a VHF radio receiver from staying tuned to the desired channel?
choices: The local oscillator frequency is beating against the incoming signal to produce an Intermediate Frequency (IF).
The output signal of the Phase Locked Loop (PLL) circuit in the frequency synthesizer has become unlocked.
The discriminator circuit is alternately developing positive and negative voltages at the modulation frequency.
The ratio detector circuit is producing a variable output that deviates across the receiver’s dynamic range.
explanation: The synthesizer's phase-locked loop holds the oscillator on the selected channel by comparing it with a crystal reference. If the PLL loses lock, the oscillator drifts and the receiver can't stay on frequency. Mixing the local oscillator with the signal to make an IF is normal operation.

stem: What fault may exist if a VHF radio receiver fails to produce audible output from the speaker and the squelch control has no effect?
choices: A component in the RF amplifier stage has failed or the signal from a preceding stage is grounded.
The Local Oscillator stage is no longer supplying a signal to the mixer stage at the correct frequency.
The AF amplifier may be defective or the transmitter Push-To-Talk circuit may be activated.
The mixer stage is no longer producing an output signal on the correct Intermediate Frequency (IF).
explanation: Squelch acts on the audio path, so if the AF amplifier is dead, opening the squelch changes nothing. A stuck Push-To-Talk circuit has the same effect, because keying the transmitter mutes the receiver. RF, mixer or oscillator faults would still leave noise audible with the squelch open.

stem: What is indicated if a VHF radio fails to receive nearby stations and a voltmeter connected between the positive side of a radio’s DC line and ground reads zero line voltage? The fuse in the VHF radio also reads zero when checked with an ohmmeter.
choices: The antenna may be defective or water intrusion has affected antenna system performance.
The coaxial transmission line may be open, shorted, or a connector has become intermittent.
A fault in the discriminator circuit is producing zero output voltage during peak modulation.
A “crowbar” circuit has prevented an over current condition that might damage the radio.
explanation: A fuse reading zero ohms is intact, so the radio didn't blow it; the DC supply itself has shut off. A crowbar protection circuit in the power supply that has fired and clamped its output removes line voltage this way, protecting the radio. Antenna, coax or discriminator faults wouldn't remove DC line voltage.

stem: What fault may exist if a VHF radio receiver fails to produce audible output from the speaker and the squelch control has no effect?
choices: The AF amplifier may be defective or the transmitter Push-To-Talk circuit may be activated.
A component in the RF amplifier stage has failed or the signal from a preceding stage is grounded.
The Local Oscillator stage is no longer supplying a signal to the mixer stage at the correct frequency.
The mixer stage is no longer producing an output signal on the correct Intermediate Frequency (IF).
explanation: With the audio amplifier dead, nothing reaches the speaker no matter where the squelch is set. A Push-To-Talk circuit stuck in transmit gives the same symptom by muting the receiver. A failed RF, mixer or local oscillator stage would remove signals but still let noise through with the squelch open.

stem: What condition may prevent a VHF radio receiver from receiving a weak signal?
choices: The local oscillator frequency is beating against the incoming signal to produce an Intermediate Frequency (IF).
The output signal of the Phase Locked Loop (PLL) circuit in the frequency synthesizer has become unlocked.
The output signal of an AF amplifier stage is greater than the input signal.
The weak RF signal has been suppressed at the limiter stage of the received by capture effect.
explanation: When a stronger signal occupies the same channel, the FM limiter captures it and suppresses the weaker one, so a weak station disappears even though the receiver is working. Producing an IF by mixing is normal, and an AF stage with more output than input is simply doing its job.

stem: Which of the following is the best test procedure to isolate the source of distortion in the audio output of a receiver?
choices: Use an oscilloscope to visually display AC signals on the output of each AF amplifier stage.
Use a spectrum analyzer to visually display the amplitude and frequency of each AF amplifier stage input.
Use a signal generator to inject a 1 KHz signal into the first AF amplifier stage and evaluate audio output.
Use a digital voltmeter to measure transistor bias voltages in each AF amplifier stage.
explanation: Signal tracing with an oscilloscope shows the actual audio waveform at the output of each AF stage, so the stage where clean audio first turns distorted identifies the fault. Measuring bias or judging only the final speaker output doesn't pinpoint which stage is distorting.

stem: What condition may cause a significant loss in VHF receiver sensitivity?
choices: A reading of 9.6 when a voltmeter is connected between the positive side of the radio’s DC line and ground.
The presence of a -90dbm signal measured at the 2nd IF output with the receiver tuned to the desired input frequency.
An internal signal that is very weak in comparison to the desired signal at the output of the second IF stage.
Replacing (75 ohm) RG-59/U coaxial transmission line with a (50 ohm) RG-8/U or LMR-400 Ultraflex cable.
explanation: A 12 V marine radio normally runs on about 12.8 to 13.8 V DC. A reading of only 9.6 V starves the receiver stages, reducing gain and sensitivity. Replacing 75 Ω RG-59/U with 50 Ω RG-8/U or LMR-400 would actually improve the match and cut line loss.

stem: Which of the following test procedures may be used to determine a VHF receiver’s minimum discernible signal?
choices: Connect an oscilliscope to the antenna input and observe the amplitude of minimum signal voltage plotted on the display’s vertical axis as a function of time on the horizontal axis.

Set a signal generator to the frequency of the VHF receiver, adjust the output signal to near zero, and increase the signal level until an audio voltmeter connected to the AF output point indicates a 3-dB increase.

Connect a spectrum analyzer to the antenna input and apply the maximum amount of attentuation to detect minimum signal level plotted on the display’s vertical axis as a function of frequency on the horizontal axis.
Connect a 156.3 Mhz signal generator to the antenna input, set the VHF receiver to channel 06 and measure dynamic range using an oscilliscope.
explanation: Minimum discernible signal is the input level equal to the receiver's own noise floor. Starting near zero, raise the generator output until the AF output rises 3 dB above noise alone; signal plus noise is then twice the noise power, so that input level is the MDS.

stem: Which of the following procedures may be used in many U.S. ports as a quick field test to determine if a shipboard VHF receiver is operating properly?
choices: Tune the VHF receiver to 158.6 MHz and listen for local U.S. Coast Guard announcements or radio traffic from other vessels.
Set the VHF radio to a simplex channel, key the transmitter, and monitor the quality of the transmitted signal with the internal receiver.
Tune the VHF radio to 162.550 MHz, 162.400 MHz or 162.475 MHz and listen for broadcasts from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Connect appropriate test equipment to the radio and measure signal levels at the output of the receiver’s RF amplifier stage.
explanation: NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts continuously on 162.550, 162.400 and 162.475 MHz (WX1, WX2 and WX3) along most U.S. coasts, so tuning one in is a quick, reliable receiver check. A radio can't monitor its own transmission, because the receiver is muted while transmitting.

stem: What ohmmeter reading may indicate a faulty component in a VHF receiver?
choices: Low resistance across a diode in one direction, high resistance when test leads are reversed.
Zero ohms across an in-line fuse in a DC power circuit.
Infinite ohms across a ceramic bypass capacitor in a transistor amplifier circuit.
A transistor indicates low resistance between emitter and base when test leads are reversed across them.
explanation: A good base-emitter junction acts like a diode: low resistance one way, high resistance with the leads reversed. Low resistance in both directions means the junction is shorted. Zero ohms across a good fuse and infinite ohms across a bypass capacitor are normal readings.

stem: What condition may indicate a VHF receiver fault?
choices: The same voltage reading between each lead of a 100K-ohm resistor and ground in a bias circuit.
A “click” is heard when an ohmmeter set to R X 1 is touched across loudspeaker terminals.
A voltage drop across the leads of a 47K ohm resistor in an intermediate frequency amplifier stage.
The presence of an AC signal on the output of an audio frequency amplifier stage.
explanation: Current through a bias resistor normally produces a voltage drop across it. Identical voltages at both ends of a 100 kΩ bias resistor mean no current is flowing or the resistor is shorted, so the stage is improperly biased. A speaker click, a drop across a resistor, and audio at an AF output are all normal.

stem: What condition may cause noisy operation of a VHF receiver?
choices: An output signal that is larger than the input signal in an audio frequency amplifier stage.
A defective potentiometer in the audio frequency amplifier stage.
Low bias voltage to an intermediate frequency amplifier stage.
An open winding in a secondary of a coupling transformer in the audio frequency amplifier stage.
explanation: A worn or dirty potentiometer, such as the volume control in the audio stage, makes intermittent contact along its track and produces crackling, scratchy noise. An open transformer winding would kill the audio instead, and an AF stage with more output than input is normal.

stem: What is the maximum allowable deviation of a marine VHF transmitter?
choices: 12 kHz
10 kHz
7.5 kHz
5 kHz
explanation: Marine VHF voice uses 16K0G3E emission with a maximum frequency deviation of ±5 kHz. Deviating more than 5 kHz spreads the signal beyond its 16 kHz necessary bandwidth toward adjacent channels and distorts reception.

stem: What is the modulation index?
choices: The maximum carrier deviation divided by the maximum modulation frequency.
The maximum modulation frequency divided by the maximum carrier frequency.
The maximum carrier deviation multiplied by the maximum carrier frequency.
The maximum carrier deviation divided by the amount of pre-emphasis.
explanation: Modulation index compares how far the carrier swings with how fast it swings: m = Δf / f<sub>m</sub>. For example, 5 kHz deviation with a 2.5 kHz tone gives m = 5 / 2.5 = 2. The index determines how many significant sidebands an FM signal produces.

stem: How is pre-emphasis used in an FM transceiver?
choices: The lower modulation frequencies are boosted before transmitting by 3 db per octave and reduced by the same amount at the receiver.
The higher modulation frequencies are boosted before transmitting by 6 db per octave and reduced by the same amount at the receiver.
The lower modulation frequencies are boosted before transmitting by 6 db per octave and reduced by the same amount at the receiver.
The higher modulation frequencies are boosted before transmitting by 3 db per octave and reduced by the same amount at the receiver.
explanation: FM noise rises with audio frequency, so the transmitter boosts the higher audio frequencies by 6 dB per octave (pre-emphasis) and the receiver cuts them by the same 6 dB per octave (de-emphasis). Audio response ends up flat while high-frequency noise is reduced, improving signal-to-noise.

stem: A modulation index set to less than 1 to 1 may result in what?
choices: Excessive deviation
Unstable signal excursions
Unusually low level transmit audio
Unusually high pitch audio response
explanation: The modulation index reflects how hard the audio drives the carrier's deviation. An index below 1 means the deviation is small compared with the audio frequency, so the transmitter is undermodulated and the receiving station hears weak, low-level audio.

stem: What is the most common type of emission for shipboard VHF-DSC transceivers?
choices: F1B
J3B
G3E
H3E
explanation: Marine VHF voice is 16K0G3E: G is phase modulation (the indirect FM most transceivers generate), 3 is a single channel of analog information, and E is telephony. J3E and H3E are HF single-sideband modes, and F1B is direct-FSK telegraphy.

stem: How many sidebands does a VHF FM transmitter have?
choices: One
Two
One to four
Many
explanation: Frequency modulation produces pairs of sidebands at multiples of the modulating frequency on both sides of the carrier, theoretically an infinite number. Their amplitudes follow Bessel functions of the modulation index; only those within the necessary bandwidth are significant, but there are many, not just one or two.

stem: What condition may be indicated if a VHF radio is unable to contact nearby stations and an inline wattmeter indicates power outputs of 1 watt (LOW power) mode and 8.5 watts (HIGH power) mode with +12.8 vdc applied to the radio’s DC line?
choices: The AF Power Amplifier (PA) may be malfunctioning when the transmitter operates in the high power mode.
Negative feedback in the PA stage may be preventing high amplitude oscillations in the high power mode.
The transmitter output is low in the high power mode but it is still functioning within FCC specifications.
The transmitter output will increase in the high power mode with modulation between 75 and 100 percent.
explanation: FCC rules require ship VHF transmitters to deliver at least 8 W but no more than 25 W, with reduction to 1 W or less. An 8.5 W high-power reading is weaker than expected yet still legal, and the 1 W low setting is correct, so the inability to contact stations probably lies elsewhere.

stem: Antenna system matching can be analyzed by determining the Standing Wave Ratio (SWR). Which of the following is the best test procedure to measure the SWR of a marine VHF antenna system?
choices: Insert an in-line RF Power meter between the VHF radio and an artificial antenna, set the radio to any channel, key the microphone, and read the measured value.

Insert a SWR meter between the VHF transmitter and the coaxial transmission line connected to the antenna, set the radio to channel 16, and conduct a “RADIO CHECK” with a nearby U.S. Coast Guard station or vessel.

Insert an in-line RF Power meter between the VHF radio and the coaxial transmission line disconnected from the antenna, activate the Push-To-Talk (PTT) circuit, and read the forward and reflected values.

Insert a SWR meter between the VHF radio and the coaxial transmission line connected to the antenna, set the radio to an unused channel, activate the Push-To-Talk (PTT) circuit, and read the measured value.
explanation: SWR must be measured on the actual antenna system, so the meter goes between the radio and the coax feeding the antenna. Keying on an unused channel avoids interfering with other stations; a radio check on Channel 16 is improper, and a dummy load or disconnected line can't show the antenna's match.

stem: A mismatched antenna system can degrade marine VHF radio performance. Antenna system matching can be analyzed by determining the Standing Wave Ratio (SWR). Which of the following is the best test procedure to determine the VHF antenna system SWR?
choices: Insert a directional wattmeter between the VHF transmitter and the coaxial transmission line connected to the antenna, activate the Push-To-Talk (PTT) circuit, observe the measured values of forward and reflected power.

Insert a SWR meter between the VHF transmitter and the coaxial transmission line disconnected from the antenna, set the radio to an unused channel, activate the Push-To-Talk circuit, and read the measured value.
Insert a directional wattmeter between the VHF radio and an artificial antenna, set the radio to any channel, key the microphone, and read the values of forward and reflected power.

Insert an in-line RF Power meter between the VHF transmitter and the coaxial transmission line connected to a 50 ohm load, activate the Push-To-Talk (PTT) circuit, observe the measured value of reflected power.
explanation: A directional wattmeter in the line to the working antenna reads forward and reflected power, from which SWR follows: SWR = (1 + √(P<sub>r</sub>/P<sub>f</sub>)) ÷ (1 − √(P<sub>r</sub>/P<sub>f</sub>)). An artificial antenna only tests the radio, and a line disconnected from the antenna reflects everything.

stem: What may be indicated if a VHF radio operates normally but the transmitter produces nearly zero RF output in the high power mode on all marine channels?
choices: The antenna system is presenting a Standing Wave Ratio (SWR) of 1.5 to 1.0 on the desired frequency.
The SWR protection circuit in the transmitter has engaged to prevent damage to the Power Amplifier.
A “crowbar” circuit in the power supply has prevented an over current condition that might damage the radio.
A 50-ohm impedance in the antenna system is preventing the transmitter from achieving full power output.
explanation: Most VHF transmitters sense reflected power and cut output when the antenna system presents a high SWR, protecting the power amplifier transistors. Output falling to near zero on every channel while the radio otherwise works fits that foldback. A 1.5:1 SWR or a 50 Ω load is normal, and a tripped crowbar would shut down the whole radio.

stem: What condition may indicate voltage controlled oscillator failure in the synthesizer of a VHF transmitter?
choices: Low transmitter power output in the high power mode.
An out-of-lock condition in the Phased Locked-Loop circuit.
Excessive deviation in the frequency modulated output signal.
A constant transmitter power output at various modulation levels.
explanation: The VCO is the part of the synthesizer that the phase-locked loop steers onto frequency. If it fails, the loop can't bring the divided VCO output into step with the reference, so the PLL drops out of lock; many radios then display an unlock warning and inhibit transmit.

stem: What condition may exist if a VHF radio is operational in receive mode but unable to transmit?
choices: Excessive bias is being applied to switching transistors in the transmitter output stage.
The solid-state antenna relay is no longer functioning properly.
A component in the Push-To-Talk (PTT) circuit has failed.
The SWR protection circuit has engaged to prevent transmission.
explanation: Normal reception shows that power, the synthesizer and the antenna path are working. The radio switches into transmit only when the Push-To-Talk line is activated, so a failed component in that circuit keeps the transmitter from ever keying.

stem: What condition may be indicated if a VHF radio cannot contact nearby stations on any channel, an inline wattmeter indicates 25 watts output (HIGH power mode), and no modulation is heard when the transmitted signal is monitored with an external receiver?
choices: A fault in the transmitter’s Push-To-Talk circuit is causing the loss of audio.
There is an open connection in the microphone cable or connector.
The microphone’s Automatic Gain Control (AGC) has malfunctioned.
Degenerative feedback applied to the AF amplifier exceeds specifications.
explanation: A full 25 W output shows the PTT line, synthesizer and power amplifier are all working, so a carrier is going out; only the audio is missing. An open conductor in the microphone cable or connector produces exactly that unmodulated carrier, while a PTT fault would prevent any output at all.

stem: What condition may be indicated if a VHF radio cannot contact nearby stations, an inline wattmeter indicates less than 1 watt output (HIGH power mode), and nominal voltage (e.g., 12.8 vdc) is applied to the VHF radio power input line?
choices: The RF power applied to the input of the Power Amplifier (PA) stage is excessive.
There is an open connection between the radio’s PA stage and the antenna connector.
The bias voltage applied to the Power Amplifier (PA) stage may be insufficient.
A defective capacitor is blocking DC voltage from appearing at the antenna connector.
explanation: The radio has normal supply voltage, yet the power amplifier delivers under 1 W. Insufficient bias keeps the PA transistor from conducting properly, so it amplifies very little. Excess drive to the PA would raise output, not reduce it, and the antenna connector shouldn't carry DC anyway.

stem: A spectrum analyzer (SPECAN) can be a useful test instrument to troubleshoot a marine VHF radio. Which of the following is the best procedure to evaluate the input/output stages of a marine VHF transmitter?
choices: Connect the radio to the SPECAN through an in-line attenuator, apply maximum attentuation and set the radio to HIGH power. Use an inductive probe to evaluate signals at the input/output of AF transmitter stages.

Connect the radio to the SPECAN through an in-line attenuator, apply maximum attentuation and switch the radio to HIGH power. Use an inductive probe to evaluate signals at the input/output of RF transmitter stages.

Connect the radio to the SPECAN through an in-line attenuator, apply minimum attentuation and switch the radio to LOW power. Use an inductive probe to evaluate signals at the input/output of AF transmitter stages.

Connect the radio to the SPECAN through an in-line attenuator, apply maximum attentuation and switch the radio to LOW power. Use an inductive probe to evaluate signals at the input/output of RF transmitter stages.
explanation: An in-line attenuator set to maximum, together with the LOW power setting, keeps transmitter power from damaging the analyzer's sensitive input. An inductive probe can then sample the input and output of each RF stage to show where the RF signal is lost, weakened or distorted.

stem: Which in-line RF power reading indicates the proper operation of a VHF marine transmitter?
choices: 25 watts forward/1.5 watts reflected.
25 watts forward/25 watts reflected.
27.5 watts forward/1.5 watts reflected.
2.5 watts forward/1.5 watts reflected.
explanation: Forward power equals the 25 W legal maximum, and 1.5 W reflected gives Γ = √(1.5/25) ≈ 0.245, so SWR = (1 + 0.245) ÷ (1 − 0.245) ≈ 1.65:1, an acceptable match. A 27.5 W reading would exceed the legal limit, and 25 W reflected means nothing reaches the antenna.

stem: What condition may cause distortion in the modulator stage of a marine VHF transmitter?
choices: The reactance modulator may be out of alignment.
The excessive use of pre-emphasis on audio signals above 25 kHz.
A defective varactor diode in the transmitter’s voltage controlled oscillator.
Transmitter modulation in excess of 150%.
explanation: In marine FM, 100% modulation corresponds to the 5 kHz maximum deviation. At 150% the carrier swings about 7.5 kHz, more than the receiver's IF passband and detector handle cleanly, so the audio distorts and the signal splatters toward adjacent channels.

stem: What terms are used to describe a device used to test the RF power output of a marine VHF transmitter without emitting a signal on the air?
choices: Dummy load, artificial antenna.
Phantom Antenna, dummy load.
Isotropic suppressor, artificial antenna.
Artificial attenuator, dummy load.
explanation: A dummy load, also called an artificial antenna, is a non-inductive 50 Ω resistor that absorbs transmitter power as heat. It gives the transmitter a matched load so power output can be measured without radiating a signal.

stem: What is the correct frequency shift and sub-carrier for VHF-DSC?
choices: 1300-2100 Hz, sub-carrier 1700 Hz.
1500-2300 Hz, sub-carrier 1900 Hz.
1200-2600 Hz, sub-carrier 1900 Hz.
1500-2300 Hz, sub-carrier 1700 Hz.
explanation: VHF DSC is frequency-shift keyed audio: tones of 1300 Hz and 2100 Hz, centered on a 1700 Hz sub-carrier (1700 ± 400 Hz), modulate the transmitter on Channel 70. The 1500 to 2300 Hz pairs and the 1900 Hz sub-carrier don't match the DSC standard.

stem: What is the correct modulation rate and index of modulation for VHF-DSC?
explanation: ITU-R M.493 specifies VHF DSC signaling at 1200 baud, with the 1300/2100 Hz sub-carrier applied to the transmitter at a modulation index of 2.0 ± 10%. MF/HF DSC, by contrast, runs at only 100 baud.

stem: How might a DSC radio check be accomplished with a coast station?
choices: Enter the station's MMSI, and press the button under the red plastic cover for 5 seconds.
Select DSC menu item TEST, enter the Coast Station's FCC call letters, and send the test call.
Select DSC menu item TEST, enter the Coast Station's MMSI number, and send the test.
Select DSC menu ALL SHIPS, and send the test message.
explanation: DSC addresses stations by MMSI, not call letters, so a test call to a coast station uses the TEST menu with that station's MMSI (coast station MMSIs begin with 00). The button under the red cover sends a distress alert and must never be used for testing.

stem: You attempt to program a new MMSI into a VHF radio with an existing MMSI. The radio will not accept the entry. What is the best course of action to correct this problem?
choices: You must RESET the DSC memory by holding down two buttons as described in the user manual.
You can never change a number, once one is already programmed.
Re-register the old MMSI with the new owner and make no programming changes to the radio.
Contact the manufacturer for action to clear the MMSI memory and accept the new number.
explanation: Most DSC radios let the user enter an MMSI only once and then lock it against tampering. Clearing a stored MMSI so a new number can be entered requires the manufacturer or its authorized dealer; there is no user reset.

stem: What is the time diversity reception interval for a VHF-DSC call?
choices: 33-1/3 milliseconds
40.5 milliseconds
66-2/3 milliseconds
91 milliseconds
explanation: Each DSC character is sent twice, with four other characters transmitted between the first sending (DX) and its repeat (RX). At 1200 baud with 10-bit characters, that interval is 4 × 10 bits ÷ 1200 bits/s = 33⅓ ms, so a brief fade or noise burst won't corrupt both copies.

stem: What might a voltmeter indicate when testing a DSC circuit for an outgoing message data stream?
choices: Steady reading of 12 volts DC.
Fluctuating reading from 0 to 2 volts DC.
There will be an absence of voltage.
Voltage swing from -12 VDC to + 12 VDC.
explanation: An outgoing DSC data stream switches rapidly between logic levels, far faster than a meter can follow, so a DC voltmeter shows a low reading wandering roughly between 0 and 2 V. A steady 12 V or no voltage at all would mean no data is moving.

stem: It becomes necessary to construct a temporary VHF marine antenna. What should be the approximate length of the antenna?
choices: 10 inches
12 inches
15 inches
18 inches
explanation: A quarter-wave radiator makes a workable emergency antenna: L = 234 / f(MHz) = 234 / 156.8 ≈ 1.49 ft ≈ 18 inches. A wire or rod cut to that length and connected to the coax center conductor gives usable coverage on the marine VHF band.

stem: Which of the following best describes a VHF collinear array?
choices: An antenna with phased elements, omni directional radiation pattern, offering up to 9 db gain.
The cascade filters in the VHF radio's IF section.
A shoreside directional VHF yagi antenna.
A depth sounder phased array transducer.
explanation: A collinear array stacks half-wave elements end to end with phasing sections so their radiation adds in phase toward the horizon. That compresses the vertical pattern while keeping horizontal coverage omnidirectional, giving marine antennas gains of roughly 3 to 9 dB.

stem: A masthead antenna with a base loading coil appears shorted to an ohmmeter check. What might this indicate?
choices: Positive proof of shorted coaxial cable plugs.
May be normal for a well working shunt fed antenna system.
Immediately repair both upper and lower PL-259s.
No VHF antenna should measure a short circuit.
explanation: Many marine VHF antennas are shunt fed, with the base coil connecting the radiator to ground at DC. An ohmmeter therefore reads a short from center conductor to shield, which is normal and also drains static; it doesn't prove a shorted cable or connector.

stem: What is the most common type of coax connector used on VHF transceivers?
choices: “BNC”
“UHF”
“TNC”
explanation: Most marine VHF transceivers use the UHF-series connector: an SO-239 socket on the radio mating with a PL-259 plug on the coax. N, BNC and TNC connectors appear on some test equipment and handhelds but are less common on shipboard VHF sets.

stem: What type of coaxial cable would be most appropriate for a long transmission line run?
explanation: RG-8/U is a large-diameter 50 Ω cable with much lower loss per foot at VHF than thin cables such as RG-58/U or RG-174/U, and low loss matters most on a long run. RG-59/U is a 75 Ω cable that mismatches a 50 Ω marine radio.

stem: What is a disadvantage when using high gain VHF antennas?
choices: Poor horizontal radiation pattern.
Very high radiation pattern.
Very low radiation pattern.
Signal dropout in severe weather on small craft.
explanation: High-gain antennas get their gain by flattening the vertical radiation pattern into a narrow beam aimed at the horizon. When a small boat rolls and pitches in heavy weather, that beam tilts toward the sky or the water and signals fade in and out.

stem: What is the assigned bandwidth and channel spacing for J3E voice transmissions?
choices: 170 Hz and 300 Hz
300 Hz and 500 Hz
2.8 kHz and 3.0 kHz
3.1 kHz and 4.0 kHz
explanation: Marine SSB voice (J3E) occupies a 2.8 kHz necessary bandwidth, the 2K80J3E emission, and HF radiotelephone channels are spaced 3.0 kHz apart. The 300 Hz bandwidth and 500 Hz spacing apply to narrow-band SITOR (NBDP) channels.

stem: What is the assigned bandwidth and channel spacing for J2B SITOR (NBDP) transmissions?
choices: 3.1 kHz and 4.0 kHz
2.8 kHz and 3.0 kHz
170 Hz and 300 Hz
300 Hz and 500 Hz
explanation: SITOR (NBDP) uses 170 Hz frequency-shift keying at 100 baud, which needs only about 300 Hz of bandwidth, so narrow-band direct-printing channels are spaced 500 Hz apart. The 2.8 kHz bandwidth and 3.0 kHz spacing belong to J3E voice.

stem: What is the allowable frequency tolerance for GMDSS MF-HF transmitters?
choices: 10 Hz
15 Hz
20 Hz
30 Hz
explanation: GMDSS MF/HF transmitters must hold frequency within 10 Hz, tight enough that narrow 170 Hz-shift DSC and NBDP signals land squarely in the receiver's narrow filters and SSB voice keeps its natural pitch.

stem: Using a frequency counter with an accuracy of 2 ppm which of the following are within legal tolerance for the frequencies of 2182.0 kHz and 4125.0 kHz? The counter has a display resolution of 1 Hz.
explanation: GMDSS MF/HF transmitters must stay within 10 Hz. Readings of 2182.006 kHz and 4124.995 kHz are 6 Hz high and 5 Hz low, the pair with the most margin left for counter error; the other pairs include offsets of 9 or 10 Hz, at or near the limit, where any counter error could mean the transmitter is out of tolerance.
flag: With a 2 ppm counter the reading itself can be off by about 4.4 Hz at 2182 kHz and 8.3 Hz at 4125 kHz, so no pair is provably within the 10 Hz limit. The pool keys 2182.006 and 4124.995 kHz, the pair with the smallest offsets; choose it on the exam.

stem: Which of the following are assigned frequencies for Digital Selective Calling?
explanation: The six MF/HF DSC distress and safety frequencies are 2187.5, 4207.5, 6312, 8414.5, 12577 and 16804.5 kHz. Frequencies such as 2182, 4125 and 8291 kHz are voice channels, and 4177.5, 8376.5 and 12520 kHz are NBDP follow-on channels.

stem: What are the assigned frequencies for VOICE and SITOR (NBDP) follow on communications?
choices: VOICE: 2182 kHz, 4125 kHz, 6312 kHz, SITOR (NBDP) 4177.5 kHz, 8376.5 kHz, 12520 kHz
VOICE: 8291 kHz, 12577 kHz, 16420 kHz, SITOR (NBDP) 4125 kHz, 6268 kHz, 8376.5 kHz
VOICE: 4125 kHz, 8291 kHz, 16420 kHz, SITOR (NBDP) 2174.5 kHz, 6268 kHz, 12520 kHz
VOICE: 6215 kHz, 8414.5 kHz, 12290 kHz, SITOR (NBDP) 6268 kHz, 8291 kHz, 12520 kHz
explanation: After a DSC distress alert, voice follow-on uses 2182, 4125, 6215, 8291, 12290 and 16420 kHz, while NBDP uses 2174.5, 4177.5, 6268, 8376.5, 12520 and 16695 kHz. Frequencies such as 6312 and 8414.5 kHz are DSC channels, not follow-on channels.

stem: What is the purpose of the “R.I.T.“ control on a MF/HF transceiver?
choices: Make slight adjustments to the transmit frequency.
Make slight adjustments in the receiver frequency.
Select the proper transmitter emissions.
Select the proper paired duplex channel.
explanation: R.I.T. (receiver incremental tuning), also called the clarifier, shifts only the receive frequency by a small amount so an off-frequency SSB voice sounds natural. The transmit frequency stays on the assigned channel.

stem: What is the function of the “TUNE” button on a MF/HF transceiver?
choices: To tune in a new ITU channel.
To tune the frequency of the receiver.
To tune the antenna to the transmit frequency.
To tune the frequency of the AF amplifier.
explanation: Pressing TUNE makes the automatic antenna coupler adjust its matching network for the selected transmit frequency, usually while the transmitter sends a low-power carrier. This matches the antenna to the transmitter's 50 Ω output so full power can be delivered at low SWR.

stem: What is the purpose of the “ENTER” function.
choices: To store any incoming DSC message in memory.
To recall any previously received message.
To transmit a DSC distress alert.
To accept the previous selection or data input.
explanation: ENTER confirms a menu selection or a value just keyed in, such as an MMSI or frequency, so the radio accepts it and moves on. Distress alerts use a separate, dedicated covered button.

stem: What mode is a MF/HF transceiver operating in when “TLX” displayed?
choices: SITOR (NBDP)
SSB
DSC
AM
explanation: TLX stands for telex, the display label for SITOR (NBDP) narrow-band direct printing on an MF/HF transceiver. SSB voice, DSC and AM operation are shown with their own mode labels.

stem: Reducing the “RF Gain” control on an MF/HF transceiver has what effect?
choices: Reduces degenerative feedback to the RF amplifier stage.
Reduces volume in response to a varying RF signal input.
Reduces coupling between the receiver’s RF amplifier stages.
Reduces sensitivity of the RF amplifier stage.
explanation: The RF gain control sets the amplification of the receiver's RF stage. Turning it down reduces sensitivity, which helps when strong nearby signals or heavy noise would otherwise overload the receiver; it doesn't change feedback or interstage coupling.

stem: What is the function of an “AGC” button?
choices: To maintain a relatively constant AF output when the input signal varies.
To reduce AF output when the input signal becomes weak.
To increase the gain of the RF amplifier when the input signal is strong.
To increase RF output when the input signal becomes strong.
explanation: Automatic gain control samples the signal level and adjusts RF and IF amplifier gain, cutting gain for strong signals and raising it for weak ones. The result is a relatively constant audio output as the incoming signal fades or varies.

stem: What is the purpose of the BFO?
choices: Re-injects the carrier frequency in the receiver’s detector to demodulate the SSB signal.
Replace the missing sideband and carrier frequency.
Remove the carrier from H3E transmissions.
Inverts the SSB signal to remove interference.
explanation: A J3E signal has its carrier suppressed, so the receiver's beat frequency oscillator supplies a substitute carrier to the product detector. Mixing it with the sideband recovers the original audio. The BFO does not recreate the missing sideband.

stem: If the BFO is turned off what kind of emissions can still be received?
choices: J3E and J2B
A3E and H3E
H3E and F1B
A1A and J3E
explanation: A3E (double-sideband AM) and H3E (single sideband with full carrier) both transmit a carrier, so an ordinary envelope detector can demodulate them without the BFO. Suppressed-carrier J3E and J2B signals, and keyed modes such as A1A and F1B, need the BFO.

stem: If you are listening to another vessel’s HF transmission and it sounds garbled what should you do?
choices: Change the receive frequency to either adjacent channel.
Advise the other vessel that his transmission is faulty.
Use the “R.I.T.” or “Clarifier” control to adjust the frequency of the receiver.
Adjust the squelch control to clear up the sound quality.
explanation: Garbled SSB voice usually means the receiver is slightly off the transmitting station's frequency. The R.I.T. or clarifier control shifts the receive frequency in small steps until the voice sounds natural, without moving your transmit frequency. Squelch only mutes or unmutes the audio.

stem: What characteristics are desirable in an AGC circuit for SSB voice reception?
choices: Slow attack and decay.
Slow attack and fast decay.
Fast attack and decay.
Fast attack and slow decay.
explanation: Fast attack lets the AGC cut gain the instant a voice peak or strong signal arrives, preventing overload. Slow decay holds the gain down through the gaps between syllables and words, so background noise doesn't surge up every time the speaker pauses.

stem: What is the primary purpose of both a high and a low I.F. system in a HF receiver?
choices: Using a high first I.F. amplifier results in eliminating image signals.
Using a high first I.F. amplifier results in less intermodulation products.
Using a low first I.F. amplifier results in fewer third harmonic signals.
Using a low first I.F. amplifier results in greater signal amplification.
explanation: Image frequencies lie twice the IF away from the desired signal. A high first IF puts the image far outside the front-end passband, where it is easily rejected, and a lower second IF then provides the sharp selectivity and gain the receiver needs.

stem: How does a noise blanker circuit work in a HF receiver?
choices: A limiter circuit clips the peaks of the noise pulses.
The noise pulses are used to develop a blanking pulse for the I.F. amplifier.
The noise pulses operate on the ratio detector to blank the audio output.
A Noise blanker briefly reduces the gain of the RF amplifier when the noise pulses occur.
explanation: A noise blanker samples impulse noise such as ignition pulses, and each pulse triggers a blanking pulse that briefly gates off the IF amplifier. The receiver is silenced only for the length of the noise spike, too short to notice in the audio.

stem: The voice is garbled and unreadable on MF/HF SSB channels. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The R.I.T circuit has failed.
The first RF stage has failed.
The frequency synthesizer has failed.
The beat frequency oscillator circuit has failed.
explanation: SSB voice is intelligible only when the BFO reinserts the carrier at the correct frequency in the product detector. If the BFO fails or drifts, every SSB channel sounds garbled. A failed RF stage or synthesizer would leave signals weak or missing rather than distorted.

stem: All signals sound normal on an MF/HF receiver except one that has a very high pitched voice barely readable. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The transmitter of the abnormal signal is off frequency.
The receiver frequency synthesizer circuit is defective.
The voltage controlled oscillator has failed.
The B.F.O. circuit is faulty.
explanation: If every other station sounds normal, the receiver's BFO, synthesizer and VCO must be working. A single high-pitched, barely readable voice means that station's transmitter is off frequency; the clarifier can often compensate.

stem: You are able to hear signals in the voice/SSB mode but not in the SITOR (NBDP) mode. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The phase locked loop circuit has failed.
The 500 Hz I.F. filter has become defective.
The R.F. amplifier has failed.
The B.F.O. circuit has failed.
explanation: SITOR (NBDP) reception uses a narrow 500 Hz IF filter, while SSB voice passes through the wider 2.8 kHz filter. Since voice works, the RF amplifier, synthesizer and BFO are fine, so the fault lies in the path only NBDP uses: the 500 Hz filter.

stem: The phase locked loop circuit in an MF/HF receiver appears to be faulty. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The AGC circuit has become defective.
The Beat Frequency Oscillator is inoperative.
The Voltage Controlled Oscillator is inoperative.
The 500 Hz I.F. filter has become defective.
explanation: The voltage controlled oscillator is part of the PLL itself, the stage the loop steers onto frequency. If the VCO stops oscillating, the phase comparator has nothing to lock and the whole loop appears faulty. AGC, BFO and IF filter circuits lie outside the synthesizer loop.

stem: You are able to hear signals in the SITOR (NBDP) mode but not in the voice/SSB mode. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The B.F.O. circuit has failed.
The audio amplifier is defective.
The 2.8 kHz filter has become defective.
The R.F. amplifier has failed.
explanation: Voice/SSB reception passes through the 2.8 kHz IF filter, while NBDP uses a narrow 500 Hz filter. Since NBDP still works, the shared RF, BFO and audio stages are good, and a failed 2.8 kHz filter blocks only the voice path.

stem: The AGC function of an MF/HF receiver is inoperative. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The B.F.O. circuit has failed.
The Voltage controlled Oscillator is inoperative.
The audio amplifier is defective.
Failure of a variable gain amplifier in the RF stage.
explanation: AGC works by applying a control voltage to a variable-gain amplifier in the RF or IF stages. If that controlled amplifier fails, its gain can no longer be changed and AGC action stops. The BFO, VCO and audio amplifier don't set the receiver's gain.

stem: The MF/HF receiver fails to suppress the AF output in the absence of a sufficiently strong input signal. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The AGC circuit has failed.
The BFO circuit has failed.
The squelch circuit has failed.
The AF amplifier circuit has failed.
explanation: Squelch mutes the audio until the incoming signal exceeds a set threshold. If noise keeps passing to the speaker with no strong signal present, the squelch circuit isn't doing its job. AGC controls gain, and a failed AF amplifier would silence everything.

stem: The MF/HF receiver fails to produce any AF output. An ohmmeter reading is near zero between speaker leads. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The 3 – 30 MHz amplifier stage has failed.
The speaker is shorted out.
Excess negative feedback is reducing AF gain.
The audio amplifier stage has failed.
explanation: A loudspeaker voice coil measures only a few ohms of DC resistance, so a near-zero reading across its leads is normal and shows the speaker isn't open. With the speaker checked out, the total absence of audio points to a failed audio amplifier stage.

stem: The MF/HF transceiver produces strong AF output but no signals are heard on any frequency. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The transceiver is connected to a “Dummy Load.”
A high Standing Wave Ratio (SWR) in the antenna system.
A “crowbar” circuit in the power supply is activated.
The squelch circuit has failed.
explanation: Strong audio noise shows the receiver itself is working, yet no signals arrive on any frequency. A dummy load absorbs RF without radiating or picking anything up, so a transceiver left connected to one hears nothing but its own noise.

stem: The MF/HF transceiver produces strong AF output but no signals are heard on any frequency. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The squelch sensitivity control is set too high.
There is an open circuit in the transmission line to the antenna.
The final stage of the AF amplifier circuit has failed.
The power amplifier stage in the receiver has failed.
explanation: Strong audio noise shows the receiver and audio stages work, but an open transmission line keeps any antenna signal from reaching the receiver input, so nothing is heard on any frequency. A failed AF stage would kill the audio altogether.

stem: The MF/HF transceiver fails to produce AF output but the radio is powered on and “TX” is illuminated. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The speaker is shorted out.
A shorted Push-To-Talk circuit in the microphone.
A “crowbar” circuit in the power supply has engaged.
The final stage of the AF amplifier circuit has failed.
explanation: A lit TX indicator means the radio is in transmit, which mutes the receiver audio. A shorted Push-To-Talk circuit in the microphone holds the set in transmit continuously, so no audio comes out. A crowbar trip would shut the radio down entirely.

stem: A received signal on a MF/HF transceiver breaks up rapidly and repeatedly. The signal alternates between mid scale and zero on the “Signal” meter. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Intermittent gain in the AF amplifier circuit.
The squelch sensitivity control is set too high.
An intermittent connection between the antenna and coupler.
The AGC circuit has malfunctioned.
explanation: The signal meter reads RF signal strength ahead of the audio stages, so its swing between mid-scale and zero shows the RF signal itself is coming and going. An intermittent connection between the antenna and coupler does exactly that; AF or squelch problems wouldn't move the meter.

stem: How is a J3E signal generated?
choices: By using high-level modulation to produce a single sideband.
By using a double balanced mixer and a sideband filter.
By using the audio signal to phase modulate the carrier.
By using low level modulation and a sideband filter.
explanation: A double balanced mixer combines the audio with the carrier oscillator and cancels the carrier, leaving a double-sideband suppressed-carrier signal. A sharp sideband filter then removes the unwanted sideband, producing the single-sideband suppressed-carrier J3E emission.

stem: What would be the most likely power level to use for initial MF-HF communications?
choices: 25 watts PEP
50 watts PEP
150 watts PEP
600 watts PEP
explanation: Operators should use only the power needed. About 150 W PEP is a typical starting level for MF/HF contacts at normal working distances, and power can be raised toward the transmitter's full rating only if the other station has trouble copying.

stem: How is the lower sideband eliminated?
choices: By using a double balanced mixer to block the lower sideband.
By using a filter to pass the lower sideband and block the upper sideband.
By using a double balanced mixer to insert the carrier.
By using a filter to pass the upper sideband and block the lower sideband.
explanation: After the balanced mixer produces both sidebands, a crystal or mechanical sideband filter passes the upper sideband and blocks the lower. Marine MF/HF radiotelephony uses upper sideband, so the lower sideband is the one removed.

stem: What is the most common method of generating a SITOR (NBDP) signal on shipboard GMDSS equipment?
choices: Two alternating sidebands of 1615 Hz and 1785 Hz are offset from the carrier frequency by 1700 Hz.
The carrier frequency is alternately shifted from + 85 Hz to – 85 Hz while suppressing the sidebands.
There is one 1500 Hz sideband which is shifted from +170 Hz to – 170 Hz with a suppressed carrier.
Two alternating sidebands of 1500 Hz and 2300 Hz are offset from the carrier frequency by 1900 Hz.
explanation: Shipboard GMDSS sets usually generate NBDP by feeding audio FSK tones of 1615 Hz and 1785 Hz into the SSB transmitter. The tones sit at 1700 ± 85 Hz from the suppressed carrier, giving the standard 170 Hz shift, a J2B emission equivalent to F1B.

stem: What are the major components of a phase locked loop frequency synthesizer?
choices: Ratio detector, master oscillator, limiting amplifier and voltage controlled oscillator.
Phase comparator, loop filter, master oscillator and first mixer stage.
High pass filter, master oscillator, double balanced mixer and voltage controlled oscillator.
Master oscillator, frequency dividers, phase comparator, loop filter and voltage controlled oscillator.
explanation: The master (reference) oscillator and VCO outputs are divided down by frequency dividers and fed to a phase comparator. Its error voltage, smoothed by the loop filter, steers the VCO until the two divided frequencies match; changing the divide ratio selects the channel.

stem: What is the purpose of a phase comparator in a frequency synthesizer?
choices: Compare the divided outputs of the master oscillator and the voltage controlled oscillator.
Compare the direct outputs of the master oscillator and the voltage controlled oscillator.
Compare the direct output of the master oscillator and the divided output of the voltage controlled oscillator.
Compare the divided output of the master oscillator and the direct output of the voltage controlled oscillator.
explanation: In a PLL synthesizer, the crystal master oscillator is divided down to a reference frequency and the VCO output is divided by a programmable ratio. The phase comparator compares these two divided signals and produces an error voltage that pulls the VCO onto frequency.

stem: An MF-HF transceiver works properly on voice but not SITOR (NBDP). What is the most likely source of the problem?
choices: The 500 Hz I.F. filter has failed.
The audio amplifier has failed.
The phase locked loop circuit has failed.
The R.F. amplifier has failed.
explanation: Voice and NBDP share most of the transceiver, including the PLL, RF amplifier and audio stages. Only NBDP depends on the narrow 500 Hz IF filter, so when voice works and NBDP doesn't, that filter is the likely failure.

stem: Which of the following conditions would indicate the malfunction of a 2182 kHz radiotelephone system?
choices: No discernable traffic has been heard on the 2182 kHz during the radiotelephone silent periods.
Failure to contact another station 60 miles distant during daytime operation.
Dramatic decrease in noise level observed during night and early morning hours.
The visual indication of power to the antenna fluctuates while testing the radiotelephone alarm signal generator into an artificial antenna.
explanation: Daytime ground-wave coverage on 2182 kHz normally extends roughly 100 to 150 nautical miles, so failing to reach a station only 60 miles away points to a fault in the radiotelephone system rather than normal propagation limits.

stem: Which would be an indication of proper operation of a SSB transmitter rated at 60 watt PEP output?
choices: In SSB (J3E) voice mode, with the transmitter keyed but without speaking into the microphone, power output is indicated.
In SSB (J3E) mode, speaking into the microphone causes power meter to fluctuate slightly around the 60 watt reading.
In SITOR (NBDP) communications, the power meter can be seen fluctuating regularly from zero to the 60 watt relative output reading.
A steady indication of transmitted energy on an RF Power meter with no fluctuations when speaking into the microphone.
explanation: In ARQ the transmitter sends a 210 ms block of three characters, then stops to listen for the acknowledgement, so the power meter swings regularly between zero and full output. In J3E, by contrast, no output should appear without speech, and voice peaks vary widely rather than holding near 60 W.

stem: An MF-HF transceiver is functioning correctly in voice mode/SSB but not in SITOR (NBDP). What is the most likely source of the problem?
choices: The second I.F. amplifier has become defective.
The voltage controlled oscillator is defective.
The 2.8 kHz filter has become defective.
The 1615 kHz audio oscillator is not working.
explanation: NBDP is produced by feeding audio FSK tones of 1615 Hz and 1785 Hz into the SSB transmitter. If the oscillator generating the 1615 Hz tone fails, the transmitter can't form the NBDP signal, while voice, which doesn't use that oscillator, works normally.
flag: The keyed choice says 1615 kHz, but the NBDP (SITOR) tones are audio frequencies, 1615 Hz and 1785 Hz. The pool means the 1615 Hz audio oscillator; choose it on the exam.

stem: Which of the following conditions would be a symptom of malfunction in a 2182 kHz SSB radiotelephone?
choices: No indication of power output when speaking into the microphone.
Much higher noise level observed during daytime operation.
When testing a radiotelephone alarm on 2182 kHz into an artificial antenna, the Distress frequency watch receiver becomes un-muted, an improper testing procedure.
Failure to contact a shore station 600 nautical miles distant during daytime operation.
explanation: In J3E, speaking into the microphone should make the power meter rise with voice peaks; no indication at all means no RF is being produced. Not reaching a shore station 600 nautical miles away in daytime is normal, since daytime MF coverage is limited to ground wave.

stem: Which would indicate proper operation of a SSB transmitter rated at 60 Watt PEP output in J3E mode?
choices: In SITOR communications, the power meter can be seen fluctuating regularly from zero to the 60 watt relative output reading.
In SSB (J3E) voice mode, with the transmitter keyed but without speaking into the microphone, no power output is indicated.
In SSB (J3E) mode, speaking into the microphone causes the power meter to fluctuate well above the 60 watt reading.
A steady indication of transmitted energy on an RF power meter with no fluctuations when speaking into the microphone.
explanation: J3E suppresses the carrier, so RF output exists only when audio modulates the transmitter. Keyed but silent, a properly working SSB transmitter shows no output; with speech, the meter flickers with voice peaks up to, but not above, the 60 W PEP rating.

stem: Which of the following conditions indicate the proper operation of a 150 Watt MF/HF transmitter in the F1B ARQ mode?
choices: The RF power meter indicates constant output at a level between 125 watts and 150 watts during transmission.
The RF power meter indicates power output only when characters are typed on the NBDP keyboard.
The RF “S” meter indicates a signal level between 125 watts and 150 watts during NBDP reception.
The RF power meter indicates an output that fluctuates between 0 and 150 watts during transmission.
explanation: ARQ sends three-character blocks lasting 210 ms, then pauses so the receiving station can reply with an acknowledgement, repeating every 450 ms. The power meter therefore swings between zero and the full 150 W during transmission rather than holding steady.

stem: Which of the following conditions indicate the proper operation of a 250 Watt MF/HF transmitter in the F1B FEC mode?
choices: The RF power meter indicates constant output at a level between 225 watts and 250 watts during transmission.
The RF power meter indicates power output only when characters are typed on the NBDP keyboard.
The RF “S” meter indicates a signal level between 225 watts and 250 watts during NBDP reception.
The RF power meter indicates an output that fluctuates between 0 and 250 watts during transmission.
explanation: In FEC (broadcast) mode the transmitter sends continuously, each character twice, without waiting for acknowledgements. FSK has a constant envelope, so a healthy 250 W transmitter shows a steady reading near its rated power, here 225 to 250 W.

stem: Which of the following conditions could cause very low RF output in a MF/HF transmitter operating in the F1B FEC mode?
choices: Failure of a voltage controlled oscillator in the IF amplifier stage.
A high Standing Wave Ratio (SWR) in the antenna system.
The connection of a transceiver is connected to a “Dummy Load” antenna.
Failure of a SSB bandpass filter in the stage preceding the RF amplifier.
explanation: A high SWR reflects much of the power back toward the transmitter, and its protection circuit reduces output to save the power amplifier. A dummy load is a matched 50 Ω termination and would let the transmitter deliver full output.

stem: which of the following troubleshooting methods is not valid for finding the fault in a MF/HF transmitter operating in the F1B FEC mode?
choices: Visual inspection of the transmitter (control settings, signs of physical damage or overheating, etc.)
Power supply testing with a DVM to ensure all prescribed operating voltages are within acceptable limits.
Modulation testing with a RF spectrum analyzer to measure frequency deviation in the transmit mode.
Input/Output checks with a 10:1 oscilloscope probe to identify any points of severe signal degradation.
explanation: An F1B signal simply shifts between two fixed frequencies 170 Hz apart, so frequency deviation, an FM voice measurement, isn't a meaningful test for locating the fault. Visual inspection, DVM checks of supply voltages, and signal tracing with a 10:1 oscilloscope probe are all valid troubleshooting steps.

stem: Which of the following conditions could cause zero RF output in a MF/HF transmitter operating in the F1B FEC mode?
choices: The connection of a transceiver is connected to a “Dummy Load” antenna.
The failure of the voice bandpass filter in the stage preceding the RF amplifier.
The activation of a “crowbar” circuit in the power supply to prevent an unregulated voltage increase.
The generation of a positive VCO feedback signal to a Phase Locked Loop circuit in the transmitter.
explanation: A crowbar circuit protects the equipment from a voltage surge by shorting the power supply output, blowing a fuse or shutting the supply down. With no DC power reaching the transmitter, RF output drops to zero. A dummy load would still show full output on the meter.

stem: Which of the following conditions indicate improper operation of a 150 Watt MF/HF transmitter in the F1B FEC mode?
choices: The RF power meter indicates constant output at a level between 125 watts and 150 watts during transmission.
The SWR meter indicates 125 watts forward RF power and 5 watts reflected RF power during transmission.
The RF “S” meter fluctuates depending on the strength of the received signal during NBDP reception.
The RF power meter indicates an output that fluctuates between 0 and 150 watts during transmission.
explanation: FEC transmits continuously with a constant-envelope FSK signal, so output should hold steady near rated power; swinging between 0 and 150 W is normal for ARQ but a fault in FEC. By contrast, 125 W forward with 5 W reflected gives Γ = √(5/125) = 0.2 and SWR = 1.2 / 0.8 = 1.5:1, which is acceptable.

stem: What precedes the phasing signal in a DSC distress alert call?
choices: An alternating dot pattern of 20 bits
An alternating dot pattern of 100 bits
An alternating dot pattern of 200 bits
An alternating dot pattern of 400 bits
explanation: A DSC distress alert begins with a 200-bit dot pattern of alternating 1s and 0s, which at the MF/HF rate of 100 baud lasts 2 seconds. That gives scanning DSC watch receivers time to stop on the channel and achieve bit synchronization before the phasing sequence arrives.

stem: What type of code is used for DSC transmissions?
choices: A 7 bit code with a constant ratio of 4/3 between the 1s and 0s.
A 7 bit code followed by an error check character at the end.
A 10 bit code followed by an error check character at the end.
A 10 bit code with 7 bits used for information and 3 bits used for error correction.
explanation: Each DSC character is a 10-bit word: 7 information bits followed by 3 check bits giving the count of 0 bits in the information part, which lets the receiver verify every character. A fixed 4:3 ratio of 1s to 0s is the 7-bit SITOR code, not DSC.

stem: What is the correct frequency shift and sub-carrier for MF-HF-DSC?
choices: +/- 85 Hz and 1700 Hz
+/- 170 Hz and 1700 Hz
+/- 250 Hz and 1500 Hz
+/- 400 Hz and 1900 Hz
explanation: MF/HF DSC uses 170 Hz frequency-shift keying: the tones are 1700 Hz ± 85 Hz (1615 and 1785 Hz) on a 1700 Hz sub-carrier, sent through the SSB transmitter at 100 baud. The 1300/2100 Hz tones belong to VHF DSC.

stem: What is the time diversity reception interval for a MF-HF-DSC call?
choices: 33-1/3 milliseconds
400 milliseconds
450 milliseconds
250 milliseconds
explanation: MF/HF DSC repeats each character with four other characters between the first sending and the repeat. At 100 baud with 10-bit characters: 4 × 10 bits ÷ 100 bits/s = 400 ms, long enough that a brief fade or static crash is unlikely to wipe out both copies.

stem: A MF/HF Distress priority DSC call may be formatted to include the following:
choices: MMSI, vessel position, nature of distress, follow-on communications by J3E only.
MMSI, vessel position, nature of distress, follow-on communications by J3E or F1B.
Call sign, vessel position, nature of distress, follow-on communications by J3E or F1B.
Name of vessel, vessel position, nature of distress, follow-on communications by J3E or F1B.
explanation: An MF/HF distress alert automatically carries the ship's MMSI and can include position, nature of distress and the type of follow-on communications, either J3E voice or F1B NBDP telex. DSC identifies ships by MMSI, not by call sign or vessel name.

stem: What statement is false concerning DSC calls addressed to MMSI 003669999?
choices: MMSI 003669999 is an established group call that includes all U.S. Coast Guard Stations.
DSC calls to MMSI 003669999 will be received by all DSC-equipped USCG coast stations within radio range.
DSC calls to MMSI 003669999 may not be used to test MF/HF DSC equipment aboard ships.
DSC calls to MMSI 003669999 may result in an automated acknowledgement from USCG coast stations.
explanation: MMSI 003669999 is the group identity for U.S. Coast Guard coast stations, and the Coast Guard accepts MF/HF DSC test calls sent to it; its stations may return an automated acknowledgement. The claim that these calls may not be used to test shipboard MF/HF DSC equipment is therefore false.

stem: Which of the following statements concerning SITOR (NBDP) communications is true?
choices: In ARQ, each character is transmitted twice, about 250 milliseconds apart.
In ARQ, the "information sending station" will transmit a block of three characters that the receiving station will subsequently acknowledge or request it to be retransmitted.
In ARQ, the "information sending station" transmits a block of three characters twice, about 250 milliseconds apart.
SITOR communications can be used to contact a NAVTEX transmitting station when requesting a repeat transmission of a missed NAVTEX message.
explanation: ARQ is a two-way, error-checked mode: the information sending station transmits blocks of three characters, and the information receiving station checks each block and either acknowledges it or requests a repeat. Sending every character twice is FEC, and NAVTEX is broadcast-only, so it can't be contacted.

stem: What statement is true regarding the exchange between two stations engaged in SITOR (NBDP) communications?
choices: In ARQ, each character is transmitted twice, with the second displaced in time from the first.

In ARQ, the "sending" station transmits a block of three characters and the "receiving" station responds with a one character Repeat Request. Following this the "transmitting" station will send a new block.

In ARQ, the ISS transmits a block of 3 characters and the IRS checks for parity. If the received block is correct a control signal is sent notifying the ISS to proceed. If the parity check fails the block must be resent.
Broadcasts of Maritime Safety Information, traffic lists, etc. can be copied by the receiving station in ARQ mode.
explanation: The ISS sends a three-character block, and the IRS checks that each character has the code's fixed 4:3 bit ratio (the parity check). A correct block brings a control signal telling the ISS to send the next block; a failed check makes the IRS request the same block again.

stem: Which of the following is true of SITOR (NBDP) ARQ mode:
choices: The ship station sends a group of 3 characters twice and then waits for an "RQ" signal to indicate proper receipt before transmission of the next 3 characters.
The Ship station sends each character twice, using a time diversity system to ensure proper parity.
The ship station sends a group of 3 characters, the shore station checks for proper parity and then requests the same group be resent to enable error correction.
The ship station sends a group of 3 characters, the shore station checks for proper parity. If parity is OK, the shore station indicates readiness for transmission of the next 3 characters.
explanation: In ARQ the ship sends one three-character group, and the shore station checks its parity. If the group checks good, the shore station signals readiness for the next group; only a failed check brings a request to repeat. Sending each character twice belongs to FEC, not ARQ.

stem: Which of the following keystrokes or characters follows most commands in ARQ communications when working an automated Coast Station?
choices: GA+?
ENTER
END
explanation: Automated coast stations treat the plus sign as the end-of-command marker, much like pressing Enter, so commands such as HELP+, MSG+ or DIRTLX…+ all finish with +. The station acts on the command once the + arrives.

stem: Which characters are sent by the ship station to indicate a desire to send a message via a direct connection to a shoreside TELEX subscriber?
choices: MSG+
AMV+
OPR+
DIRTLX0xxyyyy+
explanation: DIRTLX requests a direct telex connection, followed by the shore subscriber's telex number and the + that ends the command. MSG+ retrieves waiting messages, AMV+ sends an AMVER report, and OPR+ calls the coast station operator.

stem: What are the characters that are transmitted to terminate a direct TELEX connection in SITOR (NBDP) operations?
choices: KKKK
END+
EOM
explanation: KKKK tells the coast station to clear the land-line telex connection to the shore subscriber, ending the direct telex link while the radio circuit can stay up for further commands.

stem: If a vessel is within range of NAVTEX broadcasts and both the Inmarsat-C and the NAVTEX receiver are inoperative the GMDSS operator should:
choices: Select 518 kHz FEC TELEX on the MF/HF console to receive MSI.
Select 518 kHz ARQ TELEX on the MF/HF console to receive MSI.
Request repairs of the Sat-C system and wait until within range of NAVTEX.
Select an HF MSI frequency and ARQ TELEX mode to receive MSI.
explanation: NAVTEX MSI is broadcast on 518 kHz in SITOR (NBDP) FEC mode, a one-way transmission any receiver can copy without replying. Tuning the MF/HF NBDP receiver to 518 kHz in FEC stands in for the failed NAVTEX receiver; ARQ needs a two-way link and can't copy a broadcast.

stem: The sequence ARQ, FEC, SFEC best corresponds to which of the following sequences?
choices: One-way communications to a single station, one-way communications to all stations, two-way communications.
Two way communications, one-way communications to all stations, one-way communications to a single station.
One-way communications to all stations, two-way communications, one-way communications to a single station.
Two way communications, One way communications to a single station, One way communications to all stations.
explanation: ARQ is two-way, error-correcting traffic between two linked stations. FEC (collective) broadcasts one way to all stations, and selective FEC (SFEC) sends one way to a single addressed station, which receives without transmitting.

stem: Selective FEC communications (SFEC) are employed when:
choices: Multiple stations without a group SELCALL must receive communications without using their transmitters.
Multiple stations must receive communications by using their transmitters to achieve phasing.
An individual station must receive communications without transmitting (Radio Silence).
An individual station must receive communications by using their transmitter to achieve phasing and block other stations from breaking in.
explanation: Selective FEC addresses one particular station, which copies the message without transmitting any acknowledgements. That suits a ship that must keep radio silence or can't transmit, unlike ARQ, which requires the receiving station to reply.

stem: Which of the following is true of SITOR (NBDP) Mode B (FEC), in the presence of static crashes.
choices: Data flow rate depends on signal propagation.
Idle characters are sent upon request.
Transmitter and receiver cannot synchronize.
FEC reduces the error rate by transmitting each character twice.
explanation: In FEC each character is transmitted twice, separated in time, and the receiver compares both copies. If a static crash corrupts one, the other is used, sharply reducing the error rate without any reply from the receiving station.

stem: If the vessel is beyond range of NAVTEX broadcasts and the Sat-C system fails, the GMDSS operator must:
choices: Select an HF MSI frequency and FEC TELEX mode to receive MSI.
Select 518 kHz ARQ TELEX on the MF/HF console to receive MSI.
Request repairs of the Sat-C system and wait until within range of NAVTEX.
Select 518 kHz FEC TELEX on the MF/HF console to receive MSI.
explanation: Beyond NAVTEX range, MSI is still broadcast in NBDP on the HF MSI frequencies. Since MSI is one-way, the MF/HF receiver must be set to FEC (broadcast) mode; ARQ needs a two-way link, and 518 kHz NAVTEX is out of range.

stem: If the vessel is experiencing atmospheric interference with NAVTEX broadcasts, especially in the tropics, the GMDSS operator should:
choices: Select one of the 6 HF MSI frequencies and set-up the transceiver in ARQ TELEX mode.
Select one of the 8 HF MSI frequencies and set-up the transceiver in FEC TELEX mode.
Select one of the 6 MF MSI frequencies and set-up the transceiver in FEC TELEX mode.
Select the MF MSI frequency dedicated to tropical MSI and set-up the transceiver in FEC TELEX mode.
explanation: Tropical thunderstorm static heavily affects MF reception, including NAVTEX on 518 kHz. NBDP broadcasts on one of the eight HF MSI frequencies, from 4210 kHz to 26100.5 kHz, offer an alternative, received in FEC mode because MSI is one-way.

stem: What is the purpose of the antenna tuner?
choices: Minimizes the carrier output.
Maximizes the sidebands.
Provides for maximum VSWR.
